```{r library}
library(quorum)
```

## Why

quorum compares lenses, but a lens has to exist before it can be compared.
The question this vignette answers is the one an analyst asks before any
comparison is possible: *I have an APSIM ensemble, a cheap emulator I would
rather use than the simulator itself, and a koine pass -- none of them
came out of a flexyBayes fit, so how does each become something quorum can
even read?* The three seams below are the three answers, one on-ramp each.

## What

A `quorum_lens()` compares two things that agree on their shape: two sets
of parameter draws, or two response curves over the same grid. An APSIM
ensemble, a surrogate's predictive distribution and a koine fit each start
in a different shape of their own, so each needs its own on-ramp into the
lens vocabulary. `fb_ensemble()` and `verify_fb_ensemble()` are the
ensemble on-ramp (contract C5): they canonicalise and check a set of
parameter draws paired with a simulator's response, whatever produced it.
`fit_surrogate()` is the surrogate on-ramp (contract C7): it trains a fast,
distribution-preserving stand-in for an expensive simulator, so a mechanism
lens does not have to pay the simulator's cost on every draw. `emit_koine()`
and `koine_status()` are the koine on-ramp (contract C3): koine's own battery
battery, wrapped so its opinion reaches the same canonical parameter names a
hub fit uses. None of the three verbs below builds or compares a lens
directly -- that is *A quorum of lenses on Study A0* and *Adding a lens*'s
job -- this vignette only gets each estimate through its own door.

## Do

### Seam 1 -- ingest a simulation ensemble (contract C5)

A simulation ensemble is a set of parameter draws paired with the
simulator's response to each draw: a design matrix and a row-aligned output
matrix. `fb_ensemble()` is the canonical container; `as_fb_ensemble()`
(not called directly here) coerces a conforming producer -- a PESTO
calibration manifest, a raw `apsimx` run, a saved file -- into that same
shape, so a mechanism lens never has to know which producer it came from.
The parameter-to-output map below is synthetic, standing in for whatever an
APSIM run would have produced.

```{r ensemble}
set.seed(20260902)
g <- rbind(c(1.5, -0.8), c(0.4, 1.1)) # 2 outputs x 2 params, for illustration
theta <- cbind(p1 = runif(80, -2, 2), p2 = runif(80, -2, 2))
y <- theta %*% t(g) + matrix(rnorm(160, 0, 0.1), 80, 2L)
colnames(y) <- c("o1", "o2")

ens <- fb_ensemble(
  params = as.data.frame(theta),
  outputs = as.data.frame(y),
  provenance = list(source = "raw")
)
verify_fb_ensemble(ens)
```

`verify_fb_ensemble()` is the conformance check: it fails loudly, naming
the first violation, rather than letting a malformed ensemble reach a
surrogate fit silently.

### Seam 2 -- emulate the simulator (contract C7)

`fit_surrogate()` trains a fast stand-in for the simulator: a map from
parameters to outputs that reports a predictive *distribution*, not a point,
so a downstream calibration step can account for emulator error instead of
treating the surrogate as exact. The reference method, `"rff"`,
is a random-features Bayesian linear model. Writing $\phi(x) \in
\mathbb{R}^m$ for the random Fourier feature map of a parameter vector $x$
(Rahimi and Recht, 2007), the predictive distribution at a new point $x_*$
is Gaussian with

$$
\mathbb{E}[y \mid x_*] = \phi(x_*)^{\top} \mu_N, \qquad
\operatorname{Var}[y \mid x_*] = \frac{1}{t} + \phi(x_*)^{\top} S_N \, \phi(x_*),
$$

where $\mu_N$ and $S_N$ are the posterior mean and covariance of the linear
weights and $t$ is the noise precision; both the prior precision $a$ and $t$
are set by MacKay evidence maximisation rather than fixed by hand (Bishop,
2006, secs. 3.3, 3.5). That evidence-optimised $t$ is what makes the
reported standard deviation calibrated instead of an arbitrary ridge
parameter.

```{r surrogate}
sur <- fit_surrogate(ens)
pred_point <- predict(sur, data.frame(p1 = 1, p2 = -1))
```

```{r surrogate-kable, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(
  round(pred_point, 3),
  caption = "Predictive mean and SD at (p1, p2) = (1, -1)."
)
```

```{r fig-surrogate-vs-ensemble, eval = requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE), fig.cap = "The surrogate's predictive mean and +/- 2 SD band as p1 sweeps with p2 fixed at its ensemble mean (line and ribbon), against the ensemble's own training outputs for o1 (points). The surrogate never sees the points directly at predict time -- it interpolates the distribution it was fitted to."}
p2_fixed <- mean(theta[, "p2"])
sweep_grid <- data.frame(p1 = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 100L), p2 = p2_fixed)
pred_sweep <- predict(sur, sweep_grid)
band_df <- data.frame(
  p1 = sweep_grid$p1,
  mean = pred_sweep$o1_mean,
  lo = pred_sweep$o1_mean - 2 * pred_sweep$o1_sd,
  hi = pred_sweep$o1_mean + 2 * pred_sweep$o1_sd
)
ens_df <- data.frame(p1 = theta[, "p1"], o1 = y[, "o1"])

ggplot2::ggplot(band_df, ggplot2::aes(x = p1)) +
  ggplot2::geom_ribbon(
    ggplot2::aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "#440154", alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(ggplot2::aes(y = mean), colour = "#440154",
                     linewidth = 1) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(
    data = ens_df, ggplot2::aes(x = p1, y = o1), colour = "#21908C",
    alpha = 0.6, size = 1.6
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "p1 (p2 fixed at its ensemble mean)", y = "o1",
    title = "The surrogate against the ensemble it emulates"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal()
```

```{r fig-surrogate-skip, echo = FALSE, eval = !requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE), results = "asis"}
cat("ggplot2 is not installed; the surrogate-vs-ensemble figure is",
    "skipped.\n")
```

Richer emulators -- PESTO's Gaussian process, kernR's conditional mean
embedding -- register through `register_surrogate()` and are consumed
through exactly this same `predict()` contract; see *Distribution-preserving
surrogates* for the full loop, including inversion against observed data and
a posterior-predictive check of whether the surrogate distorted the output
distribution.

### Seam 3 -- triangulate with koine (contract C3)

koine is a stacked battery of marginal-likelihood and robust lenses, wrapped so its opinion reaches the hub's own
canonical parameter names -- an independently-derived fourth opinion that
`lens_koine()` (see *Adding a lens*) reaches directly, and that
`flexyBayes::triangulate()` compares against the Bayesian backends inside the
hub itself. `emit_koine()` carries the model into koine's own corner: a
population GLM with either a single random intercept or -- from koine 0.3.0
-- the multi-environment-trial structure of two crossed or nested random
intercepts, `(1 | variety) + (1 | trial)`, which is the shape a variety
trial actually has. Anything richer returns a typed abstention rather than a
wrong fourth opinion. `koine_status()` reports whether the slot is
currently active on the installed koine version, without requiring koine to
be installed to load this package:

```{r koine-status}
status <- koine_status()
status$activated
```

## Read

The predictive table above reports the surrogate's mean and SD at one point;
both are finite and the SD is strictly positive, which is what a
distribution-preserving prediction requires -- a surrogate that reported zero
uncertainty anywhere inside its design would be silently claiming certainty
the training ensemble does not support. The figure shows the same thing
across a sweep: the band tracks the scatter of training points, widening
only where the points themselves thin out. `status$activated` reports
`r status$activated` on this build, meaning the koine fourth opinion is live
and `emit_koine()` will attempt a real fit rather than decline outright; a
build without a compatible koine install would report `FALSE`
here, and every claim in this vignette about koine would still hold as a
description of the seam, just not as something this render exercised.

## Limits

None of the three chunks above compares two lenses against each other --
that comparison, and the independence and agreement machinery behind it, is
what *Adding a lens* and *A quorum of lenses on Study A0* exercise. The
ensemble here is synthetic, standing in for an APSIM run so this vignette
needs no external binary and no network call; a real ensemble carries the
same shape but a different, and generally larger, predictive uncertainty
once the surrogate has to interpolate a genuinely nonlinear response rather
than the near-linear toy used here.

## What to read next

*Distribution-preserving surrogates* walks the full seam-2 loop end to end --
ingest, fit, read the distribution, invert, and check -- on a small worked
example with figures. *A quorum of lenses on Study A0* and *Adding a lens*
pick up where this vignette stops: turning an ingested estimate into a lens
and comparing it against another. `?fit_surrogate`, `?fb_surrogate_ies`, and
`?fb_surrogate_ppc` document each verb's arguments and return value.

## Reproduce

Seed `20260902` for the synthetic ensemble. Package versions follow.

```{r session-info}
sessionInfo()
```

## References

Bishop, C. M. (2006). *Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning*. Springer.
Sections 3.3 (Bayesian linear regression) and 3.5 (the evidence
approximation).

Rahimi, A. and Recht, B. (2007). Random features for large-scale kernel
machines. *Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems*, 20.
